id3.title: ID3 decision tree
id3.sub: A decision tree built from scratch (entropy and information gain) predicts the crop and shows every question it asked.
id3.cluster: Your readings also sit closest to K-Means group {n}.
id3.purity: Training rows at the final node that are {crop}
id3.acc.title: Held-out accuracy
id3.acc.help: Accuracy on rows the tree never saw while learning
id3.acc.sub: Trained on {train} rows, tested on {test} unseen rows (80/20 split, the same share of every crop).
id3.path.title: Decision path for your readings
id3.path.sub: Each step is one question the tree asked, from the top downward.
id3.path.none: The tree answered straight from the top without asking a question.
id3.path.end: The tree ends at a node where {crop} is the most common crop.
id3.alt.title: Other crops that fit
id3.alt.sub: Profile match, separate from the tree: how close your readings are to each crop's average (0 to 100).
id3.model.title: About this tree
id3.model.body: Each reading is cut into {bins} bins with the same number of records. The tree may ask at most {max} questions in a row (it used {depth}) and ends in {leaves} final nodes.
id3.hard.title: Crops the tree finds hardest
id3.how.title: How ID3 decides
id3.how.body: ID3 first sorts each reading into bins (for example rainfall: high). Then it asks the question that removes the most uncertainty (information gain), step by step, until it reaches a crop.
nb.title: Naive Bayes and ID3
nb.sub: Two different classifiers look at the same readings: a decision tree (ID3) and Gaussian Naive Bayes. Do they agree, and how sure is each one?
nb.disagree.note: Naive Bayes gives {crop} (ID3's answer) a probability of {p}.
nb.top.title: How sure is Naive Bayes?
nb.top.sub: It spreads probability over all crops; these are the six most likely.
nb.why.title: Which readings pushed Naive Bayes?
nb.why.sub: How much more typical each reading is of {winner} (right) than of {runner} (left).
nb.why.total: The bars add up to {total} = ln(odds of {winner} over {runner}), so {winner} is about {times} times more likely.
nb.worked.title: Bayes' formula with your numbers
nb.worked.sub: For {crop}, the crop Naive Bayes chose.
nb.worked.s1: ln P({crop}) = {lp} (the crop makes up {p} of the rows)
nb.worked.s4: Softmax over all {n} crops (subtract the largest score, exponentiate, divide by the sum) gives P({crop} | your values) = {p}
nb.per.title: Accuracy for each crop
nb.per.sub: Held-out accuracy on each crop's unseen rows (the same 20% for both models).
nb.per.note: Crops classified perfectly on the test rows: ID3 {id3} of {n}, Naive Bayes {nb} of {n}.
nb.how.title: How it works
nb.how.body: ID3 asks a chain of questions about binned readings and stops at a leaf; its confidence is the share of training rows at that leaf that are the winning crop. Naive Bayes keeps each crop's mean and spread for every reading, scores your values on that bell curve, multiplies the seven scores (the naive assumption that readings are independent) by how common the crop is, and turns the scores into probabilities that add up to 1. Both are tested on the same held-out 20%.
km.title: K-Means clusters
km.sub: Groups the records into k clusters of similar soil and weather (standardised readings, k-means++ start), shown on a 2D map.
km.k.help: Use the elbow and silhouette charts below to choose a sensible k.
km.inertia.help: Sum of squared distances to the group centres. Lower = tighter groups.
km.sil.help: From -1 to 1. Higher = better separated groups.
km.var.help: Share of the information in the 7 readings that the 2D map keeps.
km.yours: Your readings are closest to group {n}.
km.yours.crop: Most common crop there: {crop} ({p} of {n} records).
km.map.title: Group map
km.map.sub: Each dot is one record, coloured by group. Your readings are the red X.
km.map.note: The 7 standardised readings are squeezed into 2 directions (PCA, by SVD), so distances on the map are only approximate.
km.prof.title: Group profiles
km.prof.sub: The average of each reading in every group, in the original units.
km.prof.note: The reading columns are the group averages (the centres).
km.crops.title: Crops in each group
km.crops.sub: Records of each crop in each group. Darker = the crop is concentrated there.
km.choose.title: Choosing k
km.choose.sub: Elbow and silhouette; the red line is your current k.
km.choose.note: Inertia always falls as k grows; pick the k where the drop starts to flatten. The silhouette is highest at k = {best} here. Weigh both, and your own judgement: a very small k often scores well but merges different crops. You are looking at k = {k}.
km.how.title: How K-Means works
km.how.body: K-Means standardises every reading, picks k starting centres (k-means++), then repeats two steps: give every record to its nearest centre, and move each centre to the average of its records, until nothing changes. The map is a PCA view: the 7 readings squeezed into the 2 directions that keep the most information.
apr.title: Apriori patterns
apr.sub: Association rules built from scratch on categorised soil, weather and crop values. These are associations in historical data, not causes or recommendations.
apr.support.help: Share of all rows that must contain the whole pattern. Each crop is only about 4.5% of the rows.
apr.conf.help: Of the rows matching the 'if' part, the share that also match the 'then' part.
apr.size.help: Bigger patterns find more detailed rules but take longer.
apr.onlyCrop: Only rules that end in a crop
apr.top.title: Strongest rules
apr.top.sub: Ranked by lift, then confidence, then support.
apr.all.title: All rules
apr.all.sub: When the 'if' part holds, the 'then' part also holds in the share of cases given by confidence. Click a heading to sort.
apr.lift.title: Top rules by lift
apr.lift.sub: Lift above 1 means the pattern appears together more often than chance.
apr.none: No rules meet these settings. Try a lower minimum support or confidence, or choose all crops.
apr.how.title: What do support, confidence and lift mean?
apr.how.body: Support: the share of all rows that contain the whole pattern. Confidence: among rows where the 'if' part holds, the share where the 'then' part also holds. Lift: confidence divided by how common the 'then' item is overall; 1 means no link, and the higher above 1, the stronger the association.
hier.title: Hierarchical clustering
hier.sub: A family tree of the 22 crops: which ones have the most similar soil and weather needs, built bottom-up (agglomerative) and top-down (DIANA).
hier.k: Cut the tree into k clusters
hier.m.ward.help: Ward: merge the two groups that add the least spread inside the new group.
hier.m.average.help: Average: the distance between groups is the mean of all pairs of crops.
hier.m.complete.help: Complete: the distance between groups is that of their furthest pair.
hier.m.single.help: Single: the distance between groups is that of their closest pair.
hier.tree.title: Dendrogram
hier.tree.sub: Read from the bottom: crops that join low are alike. Colours are the clusters from the cut; the dashed line is the cut height.
hier.clusters.title: The {k} clusters
hier.clusters.sub: Crops that end up in the same group when the tree is cut.
hier.diana.title: Divisive clustering (DIANA)
hier.diana.sub: The same crops split from the top. Each step takes the widest group and breaks off a splinter group.
hier.same: At k = {k}, DIANA and {m} linkage give the same clusters
hier.differ: At k = {k}, DIANA and {m} linkage give different clusters
hier.differ.note: They start from opposite ends, so they need not agree.
hier.how.title: How it works
hier.how.body: Every crop becomes a point: its average N, P, K, temperature, humidity, pH and rainfall, each standardised so no reading dominates. Agglomerative: begin with 22 groups of one crop and keep merging the two closest groups. The height of a merge is the distance at which it happened, and cutting the tree at a height gives k clusters. The cophenetic correlation says how faithfully the tree keeps the original distances (1 = perfectly). DIANA works the other way: the widest group is split by moving crops that are closer to a growing splinter group than to the rest.
teachers.lab.title: Technical lab
teachers.lab.body: Every algorithm has an interactive page in the technical lab (Streamlit). It starts together with the app and opens on the check you are looking at. These pages are being ported here one by one.

tip.N.low: Nitrogen is low: add nitrogen fertiliser or compost, or rotate with a legume crop.
tip.N.high: Nitrogen is high: skip extra nitrogen this season to avoid leafy growth and run-off.
tip.P.low: Phosphorus is low: add a phosphate fertiliser or well-rotted manure before sowing.
tip.P.high: Phosphorus is high: no phosphate needed; extra can lock up other nutrients.
tip.K.low: Potassium is low: add potash (muriate or sulphate of potash) or wood ash.
tip.K.high: Potassium is high: no potash needed this season.
tip.ph.low: The soil is acidic: lime or dolomite raises pH; organic matter helps buffer it.
tip.ph.high: The soil is alkaline: gypsum, sulphur or lots of organic matter help bring pH down.
tip.temperature.low: It is cooler than this crop likes: consider a later sowing date or a hardier crop.
tip.temperature.high: It is hotter than this crop likes: consider mulching, shade, or a heat-tolerant crop.
tip.humidity.low: The air is drier than this crop likes: mulch and irrigate more often.
tip.humidity.high: The air is more humid than this crop likes: widen spacing and watch for fungal disease.
tip.rainfall.low: Rainfall is lower than this crop usually gets: plan irrigation or drip watering.
tip.rainfall.high: Rainfall is higher than this crop usually gets: make sure the field drains well.
